teks.subject: science
teks.text: ask questions and define problems based on observations or information from text, phenomena, models, or investigations;

teks.subject: science

teks.kid: Be safe in the lab and field

teks.subject: science
teks.text: use tools, including calculators, microscopes, hand lenses, metric rulers, Celsius thermometers, prisms, concave and convex lenses, laser pointers, mirrors, digital scales, balances, spring scales, graduated cylinders, beakers, hot plates, meter sticks, magnets, collecting nets, notebooks, timing devices, materials for building circuits, materials to support observations of habitats or organisms such as terrariums and aquariums, and materials to support digital data collection such as computers, tablets, and cameras to observe, measure, test, and analyze information;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: collect observations and measurements as evidence;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: construct appropriate graphic organizers used to collect data, including tables, bar graphs, line graphs, tree maps, concept maps, Venn diagrams, flow charts or sequence maps, and input-output tables that show cause and effect; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: develop and use models to represent phenomena, objects, and processes or design a prototype for a solution to a problem.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: identify advantages and limitations of models such as their size, scale, properties, and materials;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: analyze data by identifying any significant features, patterns, or sources of error;
teks.kid: Find patterns and errors in data

teks.subject: science
teks.text: use mathematical calculations to compare patterns and relationships; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: evaluate experimental and engineering designs.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: develop explanations and propose solutions supported by data and models;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: communicate explanations and solutions individually and collaboratively in a variety of settings and formats; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: listen actively to others' explanations to identify relevant evidence and engage respectfully in scientific discussion.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: explain how scientific discoveries and innovative solutions to problems impact science and society; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: research and explore resources such as museums, libraries, professional organizations, private companies, online platforms, and mentors employed in a science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) field to investigate STEM careers.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: identify and use patterns to explain scientific phenomena or to design solutions;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: identify and investigate cause-and-effect relationships to explain scientific phenomena or analyze problems;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: use scale, proportion, and quantity to describe, compare, or model different systems;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: examine and model the parts of a system and their interdependence in the function of the system;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: investigate how energy flows and matter cycles through systems and how matter is conserved;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: explain the relationship between the structure and function of objects, organisms, and systems; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: explain how factors or conditions impact stability and change in objects, organisms, and systems.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: compare and contrast matter based on measurable, testable, or observable physical properties, including mass, magnetism, relative density (sinking and floating using water as a reference point), physical state (solid, liquid, gas), volume, solubility in water, and the ability to conduct or insulate thermal energy and electric energy;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: demonstrate and explain that some mixtures maintain physical properties of their substances such as iron filings and sand or sand and water;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: compare the properties of substances before and after they are combined into a solution and demonstrate that matter is conserved in solutions; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: illustrate how matter is made up of particles that are too small to be seen such as air in a balloon.
teks.kid: Matter is made of tiny particles

teks.subject: science
teks.text: investigate and explain how equal and unequal forces acting on an object cause patterns of motion and transfer of energy; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: design a simple experimental investigation that tests the effect of force on an object in a system such as a car on a ramp or a balloon rocket on a string.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: investigate and describe the transformation of energy in systems such as energy in a flashlight battery that changes from chemical energy to electrical energy to light energy;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: demonstrate that electrical energy in complete circuits can be transformed into motion, light, sound, or thermal energy and identify the requirements for a functioning electrical circuit; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: demonstrate and explain how light travels in a straight line and can be reflected, refracted, or absorbed.
teks.kid: Light: straight lines, reflect, refract, absorb

teks.subject: science
teks.text: demonstrate that Earth rotates on its axis once approximately every 24 hours and explain how that causes the day/night cycle and the appearance of the Sun moving across the sky, resulting in changes in shadow positions and shapes.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: explain how the Sun and the ocean interact in the water cycle and affect weather;
teks.kid: Sun, ocean, water cycle, and weather

teks.subject: science
teks.text: model and describe the processes that led to the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: model and identify how changes to Earth's surface by wind, water, or ice result in the formation of landforms, including deltas, canyons, and sand dunes.
teks.kid: Landforms by wind, water, or ice

teks.subject: science
teks.text: design and explain solutions such as conservation, recycling, or proper disposal to minimize environmental impact of the use of natural resources.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: observe and describe how a variety of organisms survive by interacting with biotic and abiotic factors in a healthy ecosystem;

teks.subject: science
teks.text: predict how changes in the ecosystem affect the cycling of matter and flow of energy in a food web; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: describe a healthy ecosystem and how human activities can be beneficial or harmful to an ecosystem.

teks.subject: science
teks.text: analyze the structures and functions of different species to identify how organisms survive in the same environment; and

teks.subject: science
teks.text: explain how instinctual behavioral traits such as turtle hatchlings returning to the sea and learned behavioral traits such as orcas hunting in packs increase chances of survival.

teks.subject: writing

teks.text: work collaboratively with others to develop a plan of shared responsibilities.

teks.subject: writing
teks.strand: Developing and sustaining foundational language skills
teks.text: demonstrate and apply phonetic knowledge by: (i) decoding words with consonant changes, including /t/ to /sh/ such as in select and selection and /k/ to /sh/ such as music and musician; (ii) decoding multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllable; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables; (iii) decoding words using advanced knowledge of syllable division patterns; (iv) decoding words using advanced knowledge of the influence of prefixes and suffixes on base words; and (v) identifying and reading high-frequency words from a research-based list;

teks.subject: writing
teks.strand: Developing and sustaining foundational language skills
teks.text: demonstrate and apply spelling knowledge by: (i) spelling multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables; (ii) spelling words with consonant changes, including /t/ to /sh/ such as in select and selection and /k/ to /sh/ such as music and musician; (iii) spelling multisyllabic words with multiple sound-spelling patterns; (iv) spelling words using advanced knowledge of syllable division patterns; (v) spelling words using knowledge of prefixes; and (vi) spelling words using knowledge of suffixes, including how they can change base words such as dropping e, changing y to i, and doubling final consonants; and

teks.subject: writing
teks.strand: Developing and sustaining foundational language skills
teks.text: write legibly in cursive.

teks.subject: writing
teks.strand: Developing and sustaining foundational language skills
teks.text: use print or digital resources to determine meaning, syllabication, pronunciation, and word origin;

teks.subject: writing

teks.text: use context within and beyond a sentence to determine the relevant meaning of unfamiliar words or multiple-meaning words;

teks.subject: writing
teks.strand: Developing and sustaining foundational language skills
teks.text: identify the meaning of and use words with affixes such as trans-, super-, -ive, and -logy and roots such as geo and photo; and

teks.subject: writing
teks.strand: Developing and sustaining foundational language skills
teks.text: identify, use, and explain the meaning of adages and puns.

teks.subject: writing
teks.strand: Developing and sustaining foundational language skills
teks.text: use appropriate fluency (rate, accuracy, and prosody) when reading grade-level text.

teks.text: make and correct or confirm predictions using text features, characteristics of genre, and structures;

teks.text: create mental images to deepen understanding;

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: make connections to personal experiences, ideas in other texts, and society;

teks.text: make inferences and use evidence to support understanding;

teks.text: evaluate details read to determine key ideas;

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: synthesize information to create new understanding; and

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: monitor comprehension and make adjustments such as re-reading, using background knowledge, asking questions, and annotating when understanding breaks down.

teks.subject: writing

teks.text: write responses that demonstrate understanding of texts, including comparing and contrasting ideas across a variety of sources;

teks.subject: writing

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: respond using newly acquired vocabulary as appropriate; and

teks.subject: writing

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: plan a first draft by selecting a genre for a particular topic, purpose, and audience using a range of strategies such as brainstorming, freewriting, and mapping;

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: revise drafts to improve sentence structure and word choice by adding, deleting, combining, and rearranging ideas for coherence and clarity;

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: edit drafts using standard English conventions, including: (i) complete simple and compound sentences with subject-verb agreement and avoidance of splices, run-ons, and fragments; (ii) past tense of irregular verbs; (iii) collective nouns; (iv) adjectives, including their comparative and superlative forms; (v) conjunctive adverbs; (vi) prepositions and prepositional phrases and their influence on subject-verb agreement; (vii) pronouns, including indefinite; (viii) subordinating conjunctions to form complex sentences; (ix) capitalization of abbreviations, initials, acronyms, and organizations; (x) italics and underlining for titles and emphasis and punctuation marks, including quotation marks in dialogue and commas in compound and complex sentences; and (xi) correct spelling of words with grade-appropriate orthographic patterns and rules and high-frequency words; and

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: publish written work for appropriate audiences.

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: compose literary texts such as personal narratives, fiction, and poetry using genre characteristics and craft;

teks.subject: writing

teks.subject: writing
teks.text: compose argumentative texts, including opinion essays, using genre characteristics and craft; and

teks.subject: writing

teks.subject: social_studies
teks.text: explain when, where, and why groups of people explored, colonized, and settled in the United States, including the search for religious freedom and economic gain; and

teks.subject: social_studies
teks.text: describe the accomplishments of significant individuals who settled for religious freedom and economic gain during the colonial period, including William Bradford, Anne Hutchinson, William Penn, John Smith, and Roger Williams.

teks.subject: social_studies

missions.subject: science
missions.title: World Launch: Wonder Questions
missions.prompt: Look at your empty planet. What do YOU want to find out before settlers arrive, and what problems will they face? Sort the examples, then add your own testable question and engineering problem for your world.

task.question: Sort each idea: is it a question science can test, or a problem engineers can solve?
items: Does sand or soil wash away faster on a steep hill?
How can my village get clean water from the river?
Which material keeps soup warm the longest?
How can we stop the beach from washing away?

feedback.correct: Great sorting! Questions ask 'what happens?' Problems ask 'how can we fix or build it?'
feedback.incorrect: Look again: is it asking what happens (question) or how to fix/build something (problem)?
hints: Questions often start with 'Does', 'Which', or 'What happens'.
Problems often start with 'How can we...'

missions.explainPrompt: Write one testable question and one engineering problem for YOUR world. Claim: what you want to find out. Evidence: what you noticed. Reasoning: why it matters for your world.

vocab.def: Something you wonder about that you can test or observe.
A need you can solve by designing something; say who needs it and what limits (criteria and constraints) you have.

missions.gtExtension: Write a question about your world that science CANNOT test (like 'Is my world the most beautiful?'). Explain why it is outside science.

trigger.condition: new world created (stage 1 started)
trigger.narrative: Your planet has just formed. Before the first settlers land, the Explorer Council asks what you need to find out and what problems you'll have to solve.

missions.subject: science
missions.title: Safety Station Check-In
missions.prompt: Your team wants to start testing your world's materials. Match each safety rule to the reason it protects your crew, then write one rule YOUR lab will add.

task.question: Match each lab job with the safe practice or safety equipment.
right: Wear safety goggles and pour slowly over a tray
Disconnect the battery if a wire gets hot
Stand back; only the teacher touches it; use heat-safe gloves
Tell the teacher right away and mark the area
Never point at eyes; aim only at the mirror or wall

feedback.correct: Badge earned! Safe scientists protect themselves and their team.
feedback.incorrect: Think: what could go wrong in that job, and what keeps you safe?
hints: Goggles protect eyes from splashes and sand.
A hot wire means the circuit is a short circuit.

missions.explainPrompt: Pick one investigation in your world. Claim: the biggest safety risk. Evidence: what materials you'll use. Reasoning: how your safety step prevents harm.

vocab.def: Eye protection worn whenever liquids, sand, or flying objects are used.
A path where electricity skips the device; wires can get hot.

missions.gtExtension: Write a 5-rule safety poster for a lab on your world's settlement that a younger student could follow.

trigger.condition: first lab test requested (materials or stream table)
trigger.narrative: Your first field test is about to start, and the lab chief won't hand out equipment until the team shows it can work safely.

missions.subject: science
missions.title: Pack Your Tool Belt
missions.prompt: Your survey team must measure your world. Choose the right tool for each job and explain which tool you'll use first and why.

task.question: Match each world measurement to the best tool.
left: Time a cart takes to roll
right: Digital scale or balance
Celsius thermometer
Graduated cylinder
Spring scale
Meter stick or metric ruler
Hand lens or microscope
Timing device (stopwatch)

feedback.correct: Your tool belt is ready!
feedback.incorrect: Ask: what am I measuring — mass, temperature, volume, force, length, detail, or time?
hints: Grams = scale/balance. Milliliters = graduated cylinder. Newtons = spring scale.

missions.explainPrompt: Choose 3 tools you will use in your world investigations. For each, tell what it measures and its metric unit.

vocab.def: A tool that measures mass in grams.
A tool that measures force in newtons.
A tool that measures liquid volume in milliliters.

missions.gtExtension: Pick one tool and explain a source of error it could cause (for example, reading a graduated cylinder from above instead of at eye level).

trigger.condition: survey team created and no tools assigned
trigger.narrative: Your survey team must measure the land, water, and weather of your new world—but the tool crate is unlabeled.

missions.subject: social_studies
missions.title: Mapmaker's Kit
missions.prompt: An explorer got lost in your world! Give your map the tools it needs: match each map part to its job, then add your own legend symbols, scale, compass rose, and grid, and write directions from your landing site to a landform you chose.

task.question: Match each part of the map.
task.diagramText: A world map with a box of symbols in the corner, a N-E-S-W star, a bar marked 0–10–20 km, and letters A–H across the top with numbers 1–8 down the side.
left: Box in the corner showing what each picture means
Star with N, E, S, W
Letters across the top and numbers down the side
Tiny tree picture on the map
right: Legend (key)
Compass rose
Scale
Grid system
Symbol

feedback.correct: Your map is ready for explorers!
feedback.incorrect: Ask: does it explain pictures, show direction, show distance, or help find a location?
hints: The legend explains the symbols.
A grid lets you name a box like C4.

missions.explainPrompt: Add a legend with at least 6 symbols, a compass rose, a scale bar, and a lettered/numbered grid to YOUR world map. Then write directions from your settlement to the canyon using the grid and compass rose.

vocab.def: The box that tells what map symbols mean.
Shows how map distance compares to real distance.
Shows directions: north, east, south, west.
Rows and columns that help you find exact places.

missions.gtExtension: Make a second, zoomed-in map of just your settlement with a different scale. Explain how the two scales compare.

trigger.condition: explorer placed and world map has no legend
trigger.narrative: An explorer got lost on the way to your canyon because your blueprint map has no legend, scale, or directions.

missions.subject: science
missions.title: World Materials Lab
missions.prompt: A storm is coming and your settlers need shelter fast. Test the materials you found, sort them by their properties, and explain which ones YOU will build with and why.

task.question: Sort each material by the property you tested.
items: Iron nail
Wood block
Copper wire
Foam cup
Aluminum foil
Rubber band

feedback.correct: Metals are conductors; wood, foam, and rubber are insulators.
feedback.incorrect: Most metals let energy pass through easily.
hints: Is it a metal?

missions.explainPrompt: Which material will you use for (1) electric wires and (2) the walls of homes in a cold region? Use your test data on conductivity, magnetism, density (sink/float), mass, volume, state, and solubility.

vocab.def: A trait you can observe or measure, like mass or magnetism.
Whether something sinks or floats compared to water.
Whether something dissolves in water.
Lets energy pass easily / blocks energy.

missions.gtExtension: Design a 'perfect material' for one job in your world. List its properties and explain the trade-offs.

trigger.condition: settlers placed and no shelter built
trigger.narrative: A storm is coming and your settlers need shelter. Which materials float, insulate, conduct, or dissolve?

missions.subject: math
missions.title: Rock Sample Scale
missions.prompt: Your bridge crew needs the lightest stone that will still hold. Order the sample masses, round them for the crew's report, and explain which stone you choose.

task.question: Order the samples from LEAST to GREATEST mass.
items: Sample A: 2.405 g
Sample B: 2.45 g
Sample C: 2.5 g
Sample D: 2.054 g

feedback.correct: Perfectly ordered: 2.054 < 2.405 < 2.45 < 2.5!
feedback.incorrect: Add zeros so every number has three decimal places, then compare place by place.
hints: Compare tenths first.

missions.explainPrompt: Write 2.405 in expanded notation. Round each sample to the nearest tenth. Use >, <, or = to compare two samples from YOUR world's materials data.

vocab.def: The third place after the decimal point.
Writing a number as the sum of each digit's value.
Change a number to a nearby, simpler number.

missions.gtExtension: Two samples round to the same tenth but are not equal. Find two masses like that and explain why rounding can hide differences in science data.
missions.worked: Line up place values to thousandths: A 2.405, B 2.450, C 2.500, D 2.054. Ones are all 2. Compare tenths: D has 0, A has 4, B has 4, C has 5 → D is least, C is greatest. Compare A and B at hundredths: A has 0, B has 5 → A < B. Order: 2.054 < 2.405 < 2.45 < 2.5.

trigger.condition: bridge project started and stone samples weighed
trigger.narrative: Your bridge crew needs the lightest strong stone, but the scale shows masses with lots of decimal places.

missions.subject: science
missions.title: Mixture Mine
missions.prompt: Your toolmakers need iron, and your beach sand has iron bits mixed in. Plan how YOU will separate the mixture and explain how you know each part kept its properties.

task.question: Put the separation steps in order.
items: Observe the mixture with a hand lens
Wrap a magnet in a plastic bag and pass it over the mixture
Remove the bag to drop the iron filings into a cup
Observe: the sand is still sand, the iron is still magnetic

feedback.correct: In a mixture, each substance keeps its own properties!
feedback.incorrect: Start by observing; end by checking properties.
hints: The iron is still magnetic even after being mixed.

missions.explainPrompt: Claim: iron filings and sand keep their properties in a mixture. Evidence: what happened with the magnet. Reasoning: why that proves no new substance formed.

vocab.def: Two or more substances combined that keep their own properties.
A property of some metals like iron to be pulled by a magnet.

missions.gtExtension: Create a 3-substance mixture from your world (e.g., sand, gravel, salt) and design a separation plan.

trigger.condition: toolmaker placed and no metal source
trigger.narrative: Your toolmakers need iron, and the beach sand has tiny iron bits mixed in.

missions.subject: science
missions.title: Salty Sea Solution
missions.prompt: Your settlers are thirsty and the sea is salty. Explain where the salt 'went' when it dissolved, prove the mass is still there, and propose how your town could get fresh water.

task.question: What is the mass of the salt water solution?

feedback.correct: 10 g + 200 g = 210 g. The salt is still there in tiny particles—matter is conserved!
feedback.incorrect: Dissolving doesn't destroy matter. Add the masses.
hints: Mass before = mass after.

missions.explainPrompt: Compare the properties of salt and water BEFORE and AFTER mixing (look, taste is NOT allowed, mass, can you see it?). How could you prove the salt is still there? (Hint: evaporation)

vocab.def: A mixture where one substance dissolves evenly in another.
When a substance breaks into particles too small to see and spreads out in a liquid.
Matter is not created or destroyed; total mass stays the same.

missions.gtExtension: Design a test: does stirring or water temperature change how fast salt dissolves? Name your variables.

trigger.condition: settlement placed next to ocean and no fresh water
trigger.narrative: Your settlers are thirsty, but the sea beside them is salty. Where did the salt go, and can you get it back?

missions.subject: science
missions.title: Invisible Air Particles
missions.prompt: A settler says air is 'nothing.' Use your scout balloon to prove air is matter: match each observation to what the particles are doing, then explain it in your own words.

task.question: Match the balloon model diagram.
task.diagramText: Two balloons: an empty flat balloon and a blown-up balloon with many tiny dots inside.
right: Air particles too small to see
Particles pushing outward on the balloon
Fewer air particles inside

feedback.correct: Air is made of particles too small to see—but they take up space and have mass!
feedback.incorrect: Think about what is pushing the balloon outward.
hints: A full balloon has more mass than an empty one on a sensitive balance.

missions.explainPrompt: Draw a particle model of something in your world that is invisible (air, dissolved salt, water vapor). Explain how you know the particles are there.

vocab.def: A tiny piece of matter too small to see.
Anything that has mass and takes up space.

missions.gtExtension: Model the particles in a solid, liquid, and gas in your world. What is a limitation of your dot model?

trigger.condition: scout balloon requested to survey the world
trigger.narrative: Your scouts want to inflate a balloon to look over the land. A settler says, 'Air is nothing—how can it hold the balloon up?'

missions.subject: science
missions.title: Carve, Build, Blow: Landform Lab
missions.prompt: The flood changed your world! Match each landform to the agent and process that formed it (Break/Move/Drop first, then weathering/erosion/deposition), then explain one landform YOU placed using your stream-table evidence.

task.question: Match each landform to the agent and the process that formed it.
right: Water: a river breaks and moves rock away over a long time (weathering + erosion)
Water: a river slows at the ocean and drops sediment (deposition)
Wind: moves and drops sand into hills (erosion + deposition)
Ice: a glacier scrapes and moves rock (erosion)

feedback.correct: Canyon unlocked! You matched each landform to its builder.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: was material carried away (erosion) or dropped (deposition)? Which agent: wind, water, or ice?
hints: Deltas form at a river's mouth where water slows down.
Dunes are built by wind.

missions.explainPrompt: Use the stream table (and a fan with sand in a box). Claim: how one landform in your world formed. Evidence: what you saw in your model with measurements. Reasoning: explain using break/move/drop AND weathering/erosion/deposition.

vocab.def: Breaking rock into smaller pieces.
Carrying broken rock and soil away by wind, water, or ice.
Dropping sediment in a new place.
Fan-shaped land at a river's mouth made of deposited sediment.
A deep, steep valley carved by a river.
A hill of sand built by wind.

missions.gtExtension: Your world's town is built on a delta. Predict what will happen over 100 years. Is it a good place for a town? Defend your answer.

trigger.condition: river placed and first flood event
trigger.narrative: The spring flood just roared through your world. Afterward the river is deeper in one place, the river mouth has new mud, and sand drifts across the coast road.

missions.subject: science
missions.title: Model Mirror: Strengths & Limits
missions.prompt: The council wants to use your stream-table model to predict your real river. Sort what the model can and can't show, then tell the council how far YOU would trust it and why.

task.question: Sort each statement about the stream-table model: advantage or limitation?
items: We can watch years of erosion happen in 10 minutes.
Real rivers are much bigger than the tray (scale).
We can test steep vs. gentle slopes safely.
Sand in the tray is not the same as real rock (materials/properties).
It is cheap and we can repeat it.
Real rivers have plants and ice; our tray does not.

feedback.correct: You're thinking like a model engineer!
feedback.incorrect: Ask: does this help us learn (advantage) or make the model different from the real thing (limitation)?
hints: Size, scale, properties, and materials are common limitations.

missions.explainPrompt: Choose one model you built for your world. Claim: one advantage and one limitation. Evidence: compare the model to the real thing. Reasoning: how the limitation could change your results.

vocab.def: A smaller, simpler, or different version of something real used to study it.
How the size of the model compares to the real thing.

missions.gtExtension: Redesign one of your models to fix its biggest limitation. What new limitation does your fix create?

trigger.condition: canyon formed and council asks to predict next flood
trigger.narrative: The council wants to use your 1-meter stream table to predict what the 500-km river will do. Can they trust it?

missions.subject: science
missions.title: Deep Time Layers
missions.prompt: Your miners found shells and a black layer in the canyon wall. Put the formation steps in order and explain to the miners what the black layer is and how it formed.

task.question: Order the steps that formed sedimentary rock AND fossil fuels.
items: Weathering breaks rock into sediment (break)
Water carries sediment and dead plants/animals (move)
Sediment and remains settle in layers in a swamp or sea (drop)
More layers pile on; pressure squeezes and cements them over millions of years
Sedimentary rock forms with fossils; buried remains can slowly become coal, oil, or natural gas

feedback.correct: Break → Move → Drop → Squeeze → Rock (and fossil fuels)!
feedback.incorrect: Layers form from the bottom up over a long time.
hints: Oldest layers are on the bottom.

missions.explainPrompt: Build a layered model (clay or sand layers with shell 'fossils') of your world's cliff. Describe what environment each layer shows and where your fossil fuels came from.

vocab.def: Bits of rock, sand, shells, and remains carried and dropped by wind, water, or ice.
Rock formed when layers of sediment are pressed and cemented together.
Coal, oil, or natural gas formed from ancient plants and animals buried and squeezed over millions of years.
Preserved remains or traces of an ancient living thing.

missions.gtExtension: A fish fossil is found at the top of your desert mountain. What does that tell you about your world's past?

trigger.condition: canyon wall exposed and miners find a black layer
trigger.narrative: Miners digging into your canyon wall found shells, a black layer, and stripes of rock. What story do they tell?

missions.subject: social_studies
missions.title: Regions of My World
missions.prompt: Your farmers, ranchers, and fishers each need different land. Group your world's places into regions by landform, climate, and plants, compare each to a real U.S. region, and explain who should settle where.

task.question: Match each region of your world to its physical characteristics and a real U.S. example.
right: Tall peaks, cold winters, pine forests — like the Rocky Mountains or Appalachian Mountains
Flat grassland, hot summers, few trees — like the Great Plains
Low, flat, wet land where a big river meets the sea — like where the Mississippi River reaches the Gulf
Sand dunes, hot and dry, cactus and shrubs — like the deserts of the Southwest
Huge freshwater lakes, forests, cold winters — like the Great Lakes

feedback.correct: You're thinking like a geographer!
feedback.incorrect: Look at landform, climate, and vegetation clues.
hints: Landform = shape of the land. Climate = usual weather. Vegetation = plants.

missions.explainPrompt: Create a physical-features map of your world with at least one mountain range, major river, large lake, and plain. Name them, and write which U.S. feature each is most like and why.

vocab.def: An area with features that make it alike inside and different from other areas.
Natural features such as landforms, climate, and vegetation.
The plants that grow in a place.

missions.gtExtension: Political regions are made by people. Draw one border on your map that follows a river and one that is a straight line. Explain why people choose each kind of border.

trigger.condition: 3+ landforms placed and farmers request farmland
trigger.narrative: Farmers, ranchers, and fishers need to know which parts of your world are alike. Where should each group go?

missions.subject: math
missions.title: Pin Your Landforms on the Grid
missions.prompt: Supply drones only understand coordinates. Plot the landforms you placed on the grid and write the ordered pair for each drop zone.

task.question: Which landform is 9 units right of the origin and 1 unit up?

feedback.correct: Every landform is pinned! x first (right), then y (up).
feedback.incorrect: Did you move right first, then up?
hints: Ordered pair = (x, y) = (right, up).
The origin is (0, 0), where the axes cross.

missions.explainPrompt: Write the steps for graphing an ordered pair so a younger explorer could do it. Then add 3 more places from your world to the grid and list their ordered pairs.

vocab.def: The starting point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis cross.
Two numbers (x, y) that name a point.
The across number line / the up-and-down number line; they are perpendicular.

missions.gtExtension: Your river flows in a straight line from the canyon (2, 7) to the delta (9, 1). Name one point it might pass close to and explain your reasoning.
missions.worked: Start at (0, 0). The x-coordinate (first number) tells how far to move right along the x-axis; the y-coordinate (second number) tells how far to move up, parallel to the y-axis. (9, 1): move right 9, up 1 → delta.

trigger.condition: 4+ landforms placed and supply drops requested
trigger.narrative: Supply drones must deliver to your landforms, but they only understand coordinates.

missions.subject: math
missions.title: Layer Ruler: Fraction Rock Layers
missions.prompt: Your miners need to know how deep the layers above the coal are in your cliff model. Add the layer thicknesses, then find the missing layer.

followUps.question: The whole cliff section above the coal is 2 1/2 cm. How thick is the shell layer on top of the sand and clay layers? Type a fraction or mixed number (example: 1 3/4).

feedback.incorrect: The pieces must be the same size first—find a common denominator.
hints: Twelfths work for both fourths and thirds.
Never add the denominators.

missions.explainPrompt: Measure (or make up) the thickness of 3 layers in your cliff using fractions with different denominators. Show an area or fraction-bar model and find the total thickness.

vocab.def: A shared bottom number so fraction pieces are the same size.
A whole number and a fraction together, like 1 5/12.

missions.gtExtension: If a 1 5/12 cm layer took 17 thousand years to form, about how many years did each 1/12 cm take? What assumption are you making?
missions.worked: Find a common denominator: 12. 3/4 = 9/12 and 2/3 = 8/12. 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12 cm. (5/7 is wrong because you cannot add denominators.)

trigger.condition: coal layer found in fossil cliff
trigger.narrative: Your miners want to know how deep to dig in the cliff model before they reach the coal layer.

missions.subject: writing
missions.title: Field Journal: How My Landforms Formed
missions.prompt: Settlers are worried the canyon will grow toward their homes. Write a field report explaining how YOUR landforms formed and whether the town is safe, using your stream-table evidence. First decode the science words you'll use (geo-, hydro-, -ology).

Introduction, transitions (first, next, over time, as a result), and a conclusion
Specific facts and details from my stream-table or wind-box data

At least one text feature: labeled diagram, timeline, or sidebar
At least one word with a root (geo-, -logy, trans-)
Complete sentences with correct capitalization and punctuation

feedback.correct: Your journal entry reads like a real geologist's notes!
feedback.incorrect: Check the rubric: did you include data and both simple and science words?
hints: Start with a sentence that tells your central idea.
Use transition words to show the order of the process.

missions.explainPrompt: Plan first: brainstorm or map your ideas, choose your audience (Galactic Science Council), then draft, revise, and edit.

vocab.def: The most important point of an informational text.
A word or phrase that connects ideas, like 'as a result'.
Diagrams, timelines, captions, and sidebars that help readers understand.
The main part of a word that carries meaning.
A word part added to the beginning / end of a word.

missions.gtExtension: Add a sidebar comparing your canyon to the Grand Canyon or Santa Elena Canyon (Big Bend). Cite your source.

light
the study of

missions.subject: math
missions.title: Storm Pattern Tracker
missions.prompt: A storm is filling your gauges and the river floods at 10 mm. Graph the pattern, decide which gauge is multiplicative, and find the hour you must warn the town.

task.question: Use the rule y = 3x (x = hours, y = mm of rain). Plot the points for x = 1, 2, 3, 4.

followUps.question: Gauge 2 already had 3 mm and gains 1 mm each hour (y = x + 3). Which gauge shows a MULTIPLICATIVE pattern?
The river floods when Gauge 1 passes 10 mm. After how many WHOLE hours will Gauge 1 first be over 10 mm?

feedback.correct: Pattern tracked! Multiplying makes the line climb faster.
feedback.incorrect: Use the rule: multiply the hours by 3.
hints: Make an input-output table first.
Input = x (hours), output = y (mm).

missions.explainPrompt: (Optional) Make an input-output table for both gauges. Explain how you can tell additive from multiplicative patterns in a table and on a graph.

vocab.def: Tells how to get the output from the input, like y = 3x.
Add the same number each time.
Multiply by the same number each time.

missions.gtExtension: After how many hours will the y = 3x gauge pass 20 mm? Explain using your pattern.
missions.worked: y = 3x: 3×1=3, 3×2=6, 3×3=9, 3×4=12 → (1,3),(2,6),(3,9),(4,12). y = x + 3: (1,4),(2,5),(3,6),(4,7). In y = 3x each y is 3 TIMES x (multiplicative); in y = x + 3 each y is x PLUS 3 (additive). Flood warning: 3 hours → 9 mm (not over 10); 4 hours → 12 mm (over 10), so warn the town before hour 4.

missions.subject: math
missions.title: Build the Reservoir
missions.prompt: Your capital must store rainwater. Find how much your reservoir holds and explain whether it's enough for your town.

task.question: What is the volume of the reservoir?

parts.label: What is the volume of the reservoir?

feedback.correct: 1,200 cubic meters of water storage!
feedback.incorrect: Find the base area first, then multiply by the number of layers.
hints: Volume is measured in cubic units.

missions.explainPrompt: Build a model reservoir with unit cubes. Explain why V = l × w × h and V = B × h give the same answer.

missions.worked: Base area B = 20 × 15 = 300 square meters (300 unit cubes in one layer). There are 4 layers (height 4 m). V = B × h = 300 × 4 = 1,200 cubic meters. Same as V = l × w × h = 20 × 15 × 4 = 1,200 cubic meters. Each 1 m × 1 m × 1 m unit cube = 1 cubic meter.

steps.title: Revision Station
steps.prompt: Good writers revise—they ADD, DELETE, COMBINE, or REARRANGE ideas. Here are three choppy sentences from a town report: "The dam holds water. The dam makes electricity. The dam is on the river."

task.question: Which revision combines the ideas most clearly?
options: The dam holds water. The dam makes electricity. The dam is on the river.
The dam on the river holds water and makes electricity.
The dam, it holds water, it makes electricity, it is on the river.

feedback.correct: Smooth! You combined three choppy sentences into one.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the sentence that keeps all ideas and reads smoothly.
